understand how to draw structural and displayed formulae for unbranched-chain carboxylic acids with up to four carbon atoms in the molecule, and name each compound
know that vinegar is an aqueous solution containing ethanoic acid

primer.text: From Manufacture of Ethanol you already know the two-carbon alcohol and both routes that produce it. This note follows the family one step further along: chains that end in the acid group -COOH, the recipe that sizes them, and the kitchen bottle that holds the best-known member.

lessons.title: The carboxyl group and the general formula
lessons.opening: Carboxylic acids are the family whose members carry the -COOH group at the end of a chain. This lesson fixes the functional group, the general formula and the trap inside the letter n, which counts only the alkyl chain and never the whole molecule.
keyPoints: Carboxylic acids are compounds containing the carboxyl functional group, -COOH.
The general formula is CnH2n+1COOH, which shortens to RCOOH.
The R stands for a varying hydrocarbon chain.
In the general formula, n counts only the alkyl chain, never every carbon.
Methanoic acid has n equal to zero, the classic point of confusion.

low.restatement: Carboxylic acids all carry the -COOH group at the end of a chain. The general formula CnH2n+1COOH shortens to RCOOH, where R is the chain and n counts only its carbons.
low.analogy: The -COOH group is like a family crest pinned to the end of a scarf; however long you knit the scarf, the same crest goes on the same end.
low.examPointer: When using CnH2n+1COOH, never count the acid carbon inside n; that slip is the named trap.

medium.restatement: Members carry the carboxyl functional group, -COOH, giving the general formula CnH2n+1COOH, written RCOOH for short. The letter n counts only the alkyl chain: methanoic acid has n = 0, and propanoic acid has n = 2 because one of its three carbons belongs to the group.
medium.analogy: Think of n as a headcount of passengers only: the driver seated at the fixed front end, the acid carbon, is never counted, however full the bus becomes.
medium.examPointer: Quote methanoic acid as the proof case: HCOOH has n = 0, which settles any argument about what n counts.

check.stem: Which group marks a compound as a carboxylic acid?

options.text: -COOH at the end of a chain
options.explanation: The carboxyl arrangement of atoms is the defining feature of the whole family.
An -OH alone marks an alcohol, one step short of the acid group.
That arrangement is the ester link, not the acid group.
A C=C bond marks an alkene and has nothing to do with acidity.

check.stem: In the general formula CnH2n+1COOH, what does n count?

options.text: Only the carbons in the alkyl chain
options.explanation: The acid carbon sits outside the count, which is exactly why methanoic acid has n = 0.

options.text: Every carbon in the molecule including the acid carbon
options.explanation: Counting the acid carbon would shift every formula by one carbon.
Hydrogens follow as 2n+1; n itself counts carbons in the chain.
The acid always carries two oxygens regardless of n.

check.stem: What is the value of n for methanoic acid, HCOOH?

options.text: Zero, because there is no alkyl chain at all
options.explanation: The single carbon present belongs to the acid group, so the chain count is empty.

options.text: One, because one carbon is visible in the formula
options.explanation: That one carbon is the acid carbon, which never enters the count.

options.text: Two, counting the carbon and one oxygen
options.explanation: n never counts oxygen atoms under any reading.

options.text: It is undefined for the first member
options.explanation: The formula applies cleanly; n is simply zero for the shortest member.

check.stem: What does the R stand for in the shortened formula RCOOH?

options.text: A hydrocarbon chain of any length
options.explanation: R is the placeholder for the varying chain that the acid group sits upon.
Metals appear in salts of these acids, never inside RCOOH itself.
The group is written separately as COOH; R is everything else.
Water is a product of some reactions here but is never the R group.

check.stem: Which writing of the family formula is the shortened form?

options.explanation: Replacing the chain detail with R compresses CnH2n+1COOH to its shortest honest form.
That recipe belongs to the alkane family, not to the acids.
That is the alcohol shorthand; the acids need the full -COOH.
That recipe fits alkenes, not the acid family.

lessons.title: Naming the first four acids and meeting vinegar
lessons.opening: Names follow the pattern alkan plus oic acid, so counting carbons is the whole skill. This lesson draws and names the first four unbranched members, then meets the most familiar one in the kitchen: vinegar, a watery mixture of ethanoic acid.
keyPoints: Names are built as alkan plus oic acid, such as ethanoic acid from two carbons.
The first four members are methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acid.
Their formulae run HCOOH, CH3COOH, CH3CH2COOH and CH3CH2CH2COOH.
Drawing an unbranched member means a straight chain with the -COOH at one end.
Vinegar is an aqueous solution of ethanoic acid at about 5 percent by volume.

low.restatement: Names run alkan plus oic acid: methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acid for one to four carbons. Vinegar is a weak watery mixture holding about 5 percent ethanoic acid.
low.analogy: Naming is a two-piece puzzle: the chain-length piece borrowed from the alkane world clicks onto the fixed acid ending, oic acid.
low.examPointer: Practise drawing all four members with the -COOH at the end; the exam asks for structural and displayed forms up to four carbons.

medium.restatement: Each unbranched member is named alkan plus oic acid, giving methanoic HCOOH, ethanoic CH3COOH, propanoic CH3CH2COOH and butanoic CH3CH2CH2COOH. Displayed forms show every bond to the terminal -COOH group, and vinegar counts as an aqueous solution of ethanoic acid at roughly 5 percent by volume.
medium.analogy: The four acids form one staircase of extra CH2 steps: each name climbs a carbon, and the -COOH landing stays fixed at the top.
medium.examPointer: Link vinegar to ethanoic acid by name and by percentage; the pairing is a set knowledge point.

options.explanation: Three carbons in total give the prop- stem with the oic acid ending.
Ethanoic acid carries only two carbons, CH3COOH.
Butanoic acid carries four carbons, one more than shown.
The -ol ending marks an alcohol; this structure ends in the acid group.

check.stem: Which structure belongs to butanoic acid?

options.explanation: Four carbons in total means three in the chain plus the acid carbon.
That two-carbon structure is ethanoic acid.
That single-carbon structure is methanoic acid.
That three-carbon structure is propanoic acid.

check.stem: How many carbon atoms does ethanoic acid contain in total?

options.text: Two, one in the chain and one in the acid group
options.explanation: The CH3 contributes one carbon and the -COOH contributes the other.

options.text: One, because only the CH3 is visible
options.explanation: The acid carbon is easy to miss but is present in the -COOH.
Three carbons in total would make it propanoic acid.
Four carbons in total belong to butanoic acid.

options.text: An aqueous solution of ethanoic acid at about 5 percent
options.explanation: The household liquid is a dilute watery solution of the acid, not the pure substance.
Pure ethanoic acid is a concentrated liquid, far stronger than any kitchen bottle.
Ethanol is the starting material of the acid, but vinegar contains the acid itself.
Citric acid souring fruit is a different acid; vinegar is firmly ethanoic.

check.stem: A student draws displayed formulae of the first four acids. Which rule keeps every member unbranched?

options.text: One straight chain with the -COOH group at the end
options.explanation: Unbranched members run a single chain with the acid group terminal.

options.text: The -COOH group sits in the middle of the chain
options.explanation: A mid-chain group would break the acid pattern these members follow.

options.text: Side branches appear from three carbons upward
options.explanation: The first four members carry no branches at all.

options.text: Rings form once four carbons are present
options.explanation: These acids stay open chains; rings belong to other families.

glossary.definition: The -COOH arrangement of atoms that marks a carboxylic acid and sits at the end of the chain.
A family recipe written with the letter n; for these acids it reads CnH2n+1COOH, shortened to RCOOH.
A drawing showing every atom and every bond, used here for the acids up to four carbons.
Dissolved in water; the vinegar on a shelf is a watery solution of ethanoic acid.
An aqueous solution of ethanoic acid at about 5 percent by volume.

workedExample.prompt: Use the general formula CnH2n+1COOH to find the molecular formula of propanoic acid.
steps: The name prop- means the molecule has 3 carbon atoms in total.
One carbon belongs to the -COOH group, so the alkyl chain holds 3 - 1 = 2 carbons and n = 2.
The hydrogen count on the chain follows 2 x 2 + 1 = 5, giving the structural formula C2H5COOH.
Adding the acid carbon and its two oxygens gives the molecular formula C3H6O2.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Propanoic acid is C2H5COOH, molecular formula C3H6O2.
